profile.summary: ProtT5 is a protein language model from the ProtTrans project. It reads one amino acid sequence and returns a vector for every residue, which can be averaged into a single vector for the whole protein. Those vectors are then used as the input to a smaller predictor, or the model is fine-tuned on a labelled task. The ProtTrans authors report that for per-residue prediction these embeddings beat methods that use evolutionary information, without any database search. The record here is the Prot-T5 line in the DeepProtein benchmark, which ran Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is built on the t5-3b architecture: an encoder-decoder Transformer with 24 encoder layers, 24 decoder layers, model dimension 1024 and 32 attention heads in the released config. Unlike the original T5, which denoises spans, it was pre-trained with a BART-like masked language modelling objective that masks 15 per cent of the amino acids. The tokenizer is per-residue with a vocabulary of 21 symbols, the sequence is upper-cased, the rare residues U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and training sequences were cut or padded to 512 tokens. Training started from the ProtT5-XL-BFD checkpoint rather than from scratch.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model description, Training procedure, Pretraining; config.json

quotes.text: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is based on the `t5-3b` model and was pretrained on a large corpus of protein sequences in a self-supervised fashion.
The original T5-3B model was pretrained using a span denosing objective, while this model was pre-trained with a Bart-like MLM denosing objective.
The masking probability is consistent with the original T5 training by randomly masking 15% of the amino acids in the input.
The protein sequences are uppercased and tokenized using a single space and a vocabulary size of 21. The rare amino acids "U,Z,O,B" were mapped to "X".
It was trained using ProtT5-XL-BFD model as an initial checkpoint, rather than training from scratch.

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: The developers offer the model for feature extraction or as a starting point for fine-tuning. They say fine-tuning can be more accurate than using it as a fixed feature extractor, and that for feature extraction the encoder-side embeddings should be used rather than the decoder's. All reported ProtT5-XL-U50 results in the paper come from encoder embeddings, measured in half precision, and the developers report no loss from half precision. The repository also ships a script that writes per-residue or per-protein embeddings for a FASTA file.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ProtT5 is one line in a larger ProtTrans family. The README lists ProtT5-XL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XL-BFD, ProtT5-XXL-UniRef50 and ProtT5-XXL-BFD, alongside ProtBert, ProtBert-BFD, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet and two ProtElectra models, each with a Hugging Face and a Zenodo download. The paper gives 3B parameters for the XL size and 11B for the XXL size. For ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 the weights repository holds three checkpoint files at the revision read here: pytorch_model.bin, pytorch_model_600k.bin and pytorch_model_723k.bin, each about 11.3 GB, so a result should name both the revision and which file was loaded. The README also points at a half-precision encoder-only repository, Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc, which its quick start example loads instead.

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: The record exists because the DeepProtein benchmark ran a Prot-T5 model. That paper names the checkpoint as Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50, says it is based on T5-3B, gives the embedding dimension as 1024, and used it with fixed embeddings as well as fine-tuning it per task to make their own DeepProt-T5 models.

run_guide.summary: Install the three packages the README names, then produce per-residue and per-protein ProtT5 embeddings for two short sequences.
prerequisites: Python with torch, transformers and sentencepiece, as the README installation section lists.
The README notes that a change in the T5 tokenizer can raise an error about sentencepiece_model_pb2, fixed by installing protobuf.
A GPU is optional. The README example falls back to CPU, and says half precision is GPU only and that CPU use is much slower.
Disk space for the checkpoint: each weights file in Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50 is about 11.3 GB, and the half-precision encoder repository used in the quick start is smaller.

steps.shell:
pip install torch
pip install transformers
pip install sentencepiece
pip install protobuf
steps.explanation: The first three lines are the README installation block. The fourth is the fix the README gives for the T5 tokenizer error.

steps.title: Embed two sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)
if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)
sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]
ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")
input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)
emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7]
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0)
print(emb_0.shape, emb_0_per_protein.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: This is the README quick start example, wrapped in a shell heredoc with a print of the two shapes added so the step produces visible output. It loads the half-precision encoder-only repository that the README itself uses, not the full encoder-decoder checkpoint.

steps.title: Embed a FASTA file instead
steps.explanation: The repository's own embedding script, as the README gives it. It writes an HDF5 file of per-protein embeddings; drop the per_protein flag for per-residue embeddings. The script lives in the Embedding folder of the repository at commit 27c02f07.

outputs: Step two prints the shape of the per-residue embedding matrix for the first sequence and of its per-protein mean vector; the README annotates these as 7 x 1024 and 1024.
Step three writes an HDF5 file of embeddings for every sequence in the FASTA input.

notes: The record is named Prot-T5 after the row in the DeepProtein tables; the model itself is ProtT5 from ProtTrans, and the DeepProtein paper names the checkpoint as Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50, so this page describes Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50 as the primary checkpoint and lists the XXL size as a second structured row. The pretrained weights are Academic Free License v3.0 by the README; no code licence was saved, so it is recorded as not stated. The Hugging Face card carries no licence field at all. The 3B and 11B parameter figures are the sources' own approximations, not exact counts. The paper's journal version is paywalled in IEEE TPAMI, so the arXiv PDF text layer was used; the PDF is saved as artifacts/paper.pdf and the quoted text layer as artifacts/paper.txt. The related record 09-deep-prot-t5 covers the DeepProtein authors' per-task fine-tunes of this model, and the two records should not be merged.
